To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the prevalence of hidden populations estimated with respondent‐driven samples may be biased by community structure and that this bias increases as response rates decrease.

the prevalence of a variable in the network depends on the size of the community to which an individual belongs and that low degree nodes can be undersampled in a respondent‐driven sample if the sample and population are of similar size.

the prevalence of an attribute estimated by a respondent‐driven sample depends on the size of the community in which the respondent belongs, the size of the sample, the size of network, and the response rate, and that low response rates typically induce strong biases irrespectivley of community structure.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of network communities on respondent‐driven sample estimators.
the bias that can be induced by the network structure in the respondent‐ driven sampling estimator.
the bias induced by the community structure and response rate in respondent‐driven sampled networks.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in the absence of a sampling frame, respondent‐driven methods are not a panacea for the study of hidden populations.
the bias induced by community structures is not a problem per se, but rather the result of a combination of network structure and response rate.
the bias in the RDS estimator depends on the structure of the network and the response rates, and that the RDS method is not always the best choice for hidden population studies.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the bias induced by community structures is not as strong as the bias induced by the low response rate.
the bias induced by community structures in respondent-driven sampling estimators is not as strong as that induced by low response rates.
the bias induced by community structures in the respondent‐ drived sampling estimator is not as severe as previously thought, but that the bias induced due to low response rates can be substantial.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the structure of the network and the response rates of the individuals are key elements that should be taken into account to design a respondent‐driven study.
the bias induced by respondent‐driven estimators is not only due to the response rates, as it is usually thought, but also to the community structure of the underlying social network.
the bias induced by the community structure is not necessarily larger than the one induced by the low response rates.
